items.title: Edmond "Doc" Souchon Interview, 1962-02-17
items.q: another band that they only used when they had to was Louis Armstrong's band.

ctx.x: But anyway, another band that they only used when they had to was Louis Armstrong's band. He played, you know, he wasn't the leader. But he blew so damn loud that you had to have a hall as big as the auditorium to take him. And I'm not so sure he was always on the button with his notes either. He only became good, really good, when he began playing on the Steamer. He was the president. No, what is it? The Sidney or Capitola. Yeah, yeah, yeah. The bands that we danced by, the Silverleaf, Mapleleaf, Goldleaf,…
And you mentioned the other day you'd like to tell us something about that.

items.title: Myra Menville Interview, 1958-05-07, 09
items.q: Armstrong, who was just the kid coming up at the time then, we never hired him unless we were absolutely broke

ctx.x: Well, do you think you could, as closely as possible, trace the... Use of jazz bands for entertainment from then down to now, and also the interest in it as a form of music, and the attitude of white New Orleans...

Well, I still think that today, in your audience, in spite of a very remarkable awakening within the past 10 years, which is due to the younger generation suddenly discovering jazz and accepting it, that in the old folks' mind, it still has nothing of value. It's probably degrading, and... It wasn't spoken of in polite society as anything but a nigger band for dancing. Now, as far as the type of bands, I remember that Irene Castle came to the St. Charles Hotel in around 1920, and Pierron was playing there, and…

Well, do you think you could, in some sort of chronological order, carry down from, say, 1920 to the present, the use of a white society of jazz bands for entertainment and also the recognition given to it as a value?
